tagline: Inverse-warp twist with falloff curves — from gentle whirlpools to hard tornadoes
description: Rotational distortion computed via inverse-warp so bilinear sampling stays clean at any angle. Angle sweeps ±1080° — three full rotations in either direction — for everything from a half-degree lens whisper to a tight vortex. Four falloff curves define how the rotation dies off toward the edge: Smooth (cosine bell) for organic whirlpools, Linear for a uniform cone, Hard for a flat rotation disk, and Bell (sine ring) for a twist that peaks in the middle and quiets at center and edge. Inverse mode flips the falloff so the outer ring twists and the center stays calm — a tornado profile.

faq.q: What falloff gives the most natural whirlpool look?
faq.a: Smooth. It uses a cosine bell that peaks at the center and fades to zero at the edge, matching how real vortex flows slow as they lose energy away from the drain.

faq.q: What does the Inverse toggle do?
faq.a: Inverse flips the falloff so the edge twists the most and the center stays calm. Combined with Hard falloff you get a rotating ring — useful for tornado or drill-bit effects.

faq.q: Why does bilinear sampling matter at high angles?
faq.a: At 360° or more the warp pulls source pixels from large distances. Nearest-neighbour sampling at those distances creates visible stepping on diagonal edges. Bilinear interpolates between the four nearest source pixels, keeping curves smooth even at extreme twist angles.
